title: "Other models"
resources:

The same decomposition, on models that are not biological tissue. Each family below is taken
apart into the kinds of activity of the [main page](index.qmd): a stigmergic colony over entities
and a field, a chaotic flow as one activity, agent interaction as a rewire and its laterals, and
gravity as a single lateral summed over every pair. Hover (or tab to) a title to read the exact
spec that generated it.

<h3>Stigmergy: Physarum slime (one species, a disc colony)</h3>
<p class="opk">Stigmergy has been decomposed into five activities over one kind of entity and one field: the agents deposit a trail into the field and sense it back (exchange), the field diffuses and decays under its own dynamics (field), and a move carries each agent along its heading. By composing these with different turn rates and sensor geometries we can build different transport networks out of the same five. Shown here is a single species seeded in a disc, so the colony stays a bounded circular web.</p>
<p class="opk-ref">Reference: the model is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1162/artl.2010.16.2.16202">Jones (2010), <i>Artificial Life</i> 16(2):127–153</a>, whose sense-and-deposit agent this is; the implementation we adapted is <a href="https://github.com/SebLague/Slime-Simulation">Sebastian Lague’s Slime-Simulation</a>, and the name for the mechanism is Grassé’s (1959) stigmergy.</p>
<div class="sim-gallery g3">
  <figure class="sim-card">
    <video src="gallery/slime_s.mp4" autoplay loop muted playsinline preload="metadata"></video>
    <figcaption>
      <span class="sim-name" tabindex="0">entities and a field<span class="sim-spec"><pre># slime_default -- one species, the canonical Physarum transport network.
# The monolithic `slime` operator decomposed into 5 primitives over 1 set + 1 scalar
# field: deposit (set-&gt;field) | diffuse, decay (field-&gt;field) | sense (field-&gt;set,
# turns the heading) | glide (self-propelled move). Agents spawn in a central disc;
# stigmergy grows a self-reinforcing, coarsening network.
general: {name: slime_default, seed: 0, n_frames: 400, dt: 1.0, boundary: wall}
sets:
  cell:
    n: 12000
    types:
      a: {fraction: 1.0, move_speed: 0.006, turn_speed: 0.45, sensor_angle: 28, sensor_dist: 0.025, sensor_size: 1}
fields:
  chemical: {frame: grid, res: 220, couples_to: cell}
seed:
- {op: seed_positions, at: cell, mode: disc, radius: 0.3, seed: 0}
operators:
- {op: deposit, at: cell, to: chemical, amount: 0.045}
- {op: diffuse, at: chemical, rate: 0.0175}
- {op: decay, at: chemical, rate: 0.0006}
- {op: sense, at: cell, from: chemical, cross: -1.0, noise: 1.0}
- {op: bounce, at: cell}
- {op: glide, at: cell}
schedule: [deposit, diffuse, decay, sense, bounce, glide]</pre></span></span>
      <span class="sim-cap">12,000 agents and one scalar field. Five activities: a trail deposited and sensed back (exchange), diffusion and decay (field), and a move along the heading.</span>
    </figcaption>
  </figure>

# (a fine, meandering network). Same 5 operators; only the `types:` scalars change.
general: {name: slime_curly, seed: 1, n_frames: 400, dt: 1.0, boundary: wall}
sets:
  cell:
    n: 12000
    types:

fields:

schedule: [deposit, diffuse, decay, sense, bounce, glide]</pre></span></span>

<h3>Stigmergy: Physarum slime (many species, space-filling)</h3>
<p class="opk">The same five activities, with the agents seeded across the whole field instead of in a disc and split into several species, each depositing and sensing its own trail channel while inhibiting the others. By composing them with different numbers of species we fill the plane instead of bounding a colony. Shown here are four, six and eight species, segregating into interwoven networks.</p>
<p class="opk-ref">Reference: the model is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1162/artl.2010.16.2.16202">Jones (2010), <i>Artificial Life</i> 16(2):127–153</a>, whose sense-and-deposit agent this is; the implementation we adapted is <a href="https://github.com/SebLague/Slime-Simulation">Sebastian Lague’s Slime-Simulation</a>, and the name for the mechanism is Grassé’s (1959) stigmergy.</p>

<h3>Strange attractors</h3>
<p class="opk">A dissipative chaotic flow has been decomposed into a single activity: it carries every point along its own velocity field, ẋ&nbsp;=&nbsp;f(x), where the flow f names the system, with no relation between the points at all. By composing that one activity with different flows named in the spec we get every attractor in the family. Ten of them ship. Shown here are six, each a seed cube stretched and folded until the cloud is the attractor itself.</p>
<p class="opk-ref">Reference: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0469(1963)020%3C0130:DNF%3E2.0.CO;2">Lorenz (1963), <i>J. Atmos. Sci.</i> 20:130–141</a>; <a href="https://doi.org/10.1142/S0218127499001383">Thomas (1999), <i>Int. J. Bifurc. Chaos</i> 9:1889–1905</a>; <a href="https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.50.R647">Sprott (1994), <i>Phys. Rev. E</i> 50:R647–R650</a>; <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physleta.2009.07.088">Dadras &amp; Momeni (2009), <i>Phys. Lett. A</i> 373:3637–3642</a>. The Halvorsen and Aizawa systems have no primary paper we can point at. They are catalogued rather than published, Halvorsen in Sprott’s <i>Chaos and Time-Series Analysis</i> (2003), and are named here as folklore rather than cited as literature.</p>
<div class="sim-gallery g3">
  <figure class="sim-card">
    <video src="gallery/attractor_lorenz.mp4" autoplay loop muted playsinline preload="metadata"></video>
    <figcaption>
      <span class="sim-name" tabindex="0">one activity: Lorenz<span class="sim-spec"><pre># lorenz attractor -- Lorenz (1963) convection: THE butterfly, two spiralling lobes.
# A dense `cloud` is seeded in a tiny cube inside the basin; the `attractor_flow`
# operator rides every point along dx/dt = f(x) and the chaos unfolds the seed into
# the attractor. `boundary: free` -&gt; open space (the flow is bounded by its dissipation).
general:
  name: lorenz
  seed: 0
  n_frames: 10000
  dt: 0.004
  boundary: free
  dim: 3
  world: [50.0, 50.0, 50.0]
  record_cap: 800
sets:
  cloud:
    n: 60000
    start: [0.6, 0.6, 14.6, 1.4, 1.4, 15.4]
    types:
      c: {fraction: 1.0}
fields: {}
operators:
- {op: attractor_flow, at: cloud, system: lorenz, sigma: 10.0, rho: 28.0, beta: 2.6666667}
schedule: [attractor_flow]
plotting:
  background: black
  colors:
    c: [0.24, 1.0, 0.42]
  splat_size: 1.15
  splat_res: 820
  movie_max_frames: 700
  fps: 30
  camera_zoom: 0.25
  camera_azim: 0.4
  camera_elev: 0.95
  camera_elev_end: 1.4
  camera_turns: 0.08</pre></span></span>
      <span class="sim-cap">60,000 points, one kind of entity, with no relation between them. One activity carries each along the flow. The seed unfolds into the attractor.</span>
    </figcaption>
  </figure>
  <figure class="sim-card">
    <video src="gallery/attractor_halvorsen.mp4" autoplay loop muted playsinline preload="metadata"></video>
    <figcaption>
      <span class="sim-name" tabindex="0">the same activity: Halvorsen<span class="sim-spec"><pre># halvorsen attractor -- cyclically-symmetric (x-&gt;y-&gt;z) quadratic flow: a fat three-armed folded knot.
# A dense `cloud` is seeded in a tiny cube inside the basin; the `attractor_flow`
# operator rides every point along dx/dt = f(x) and the chaos unfolds the seed into
# the attractor. `boundary: free` -&gt; open space (the flow is bounded by its dissipation).

  name: halvorsen
  seed: 0

    types:
      c: {fraction: 1.0}
fields: {}
operators:
- {op: attractor_flow, at: cloud, system: halvorsen, a: 1.4}
schedule: [attractor_flow]
plotting:
  background: black
  colors:
    c: [1.0, 0.62, 0.16]
  splat_size: 1.15
  splat_res: 820
  movie_max_frames: 700
  fps: 30
  camera_zoom: 0.25
  camera_azim: 0.5
  camera_elev: 0.7
  camera_elev_end: 1.2
  camera_turns: 0.4</pre></span></span>
      <span class="sim-cap">The same entities and the same one activity. Only the flow named in the spec differs. Halvorsen.</span>
    </figcaption>
  </figure>
  <figure class="sim-card">

    <figcaption>

# A dense `cloud` is seeded in a tiny cube inside the basin; the `attractor_flow`

<h3>Interaction &amp; flocking</h3>
<p class="opk">Agent interaction has been decomposed into a rewire that rebuilds a radius neighbour graph from the current positions, and lateral activities that act along it. By composing different laterals on that one graph we can build different collective behaviours: a per-type force law, or the three boids rules, or alignment with self-propulsion. Shown here are particles sorting themselves by type, a flock, and an ordered swarm.</p>
<p class="opk-ref">Reference: boids is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1145/37402.37406">Reynolds (1987), <i>SIGGRAPH Comput. Graph.</i> 21(4):25–34</a>, the soft-core pair potential is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.96.104302">D’Orsogna et&nbsp;al. (2006), <i>Phys. Rev. Lett.</i> 96:104302</a>, and the alignment model is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.75.1226">Vicsek et&nbsp;al. (1995), <i>Phys. Rev. Lett.</i> 75:1226–1229</a>; the implementations are adapted from <a href="https://github.com/allierc/ParticleGraph">ParticleGraph</a> (Allier et&nbsp;al.).</p>
<div class="sim-gallery">

      <span class="sim-name" tabindex="0">Rewire, then a force<span class="sim-spec"><pre># Full match to ParticleGraph arbitrary_3_1: 3 types, 30000 particles, sigma=0.005,
# max_radius=0.075, periodic, first_derivative, dt=0.1, 250 frames. Now feasible
# because attraction_repulsion runs on a radius neighbour graph (O(E)), not dense.
general:
  name: arbitrary_3
  seed: 0
  n_frames: 250
  dt: 0.1
  boundary: periodic

sets:
  particle:
    n: 30000
    types:
      t0: {fraction: 0.34, p: [1.6233, 1.0413, 1.6012, 1.5615]}
      t1: {fraction: 0.33, p: [1.7667, 1.8308, 1.0855, 1.9055]}
      t2: {fraction: 0.33, p: [1.7226, 1.7850, 1.0584, 1.8579]}

fields: {}

operators:
  - {op: radius_graph,         at: particle, radius: 0.075}
  - {op: attraction_repulsion, at: particle, sigma: 0.005}

schedule: [radius_graph, attraction_repulsion]

plotting:                      # render STYLE (read by plexus.plot; engine ignores it)
  background: black
  colormap: tab10
  point_size: 2.0

<h3>Inverse-square law: self-gravity</h3>
<p class="opk">Gravity has been decomposed into a single lateral activity summed over every pair of entities: mass, always attracting. By composing it over populations of different composition we can build different systems without ever writing a second law. Two galaxies placed among the same entities pull on each other through the same activity that condensed each of them. Shown here are a disc condensing in 2D and in 3D, a heavier central mass, four clumps merging, and two galaxies meeting on a grazing and on a head-on course.</p>
<p class="opk-ref">Reference: softened self-gravity after Philip Mocz’s <em>Create Your Own N-body Simulation</em> (2020); the encounter geometry after Toomre &amp; Toomre, <em>Galactic Bridges and Tails</em> (1972).</p>
<div class="sim-gallery g3">

# Initialization is the `seed_positions` operator: `mode: disc` places the disc, and
# `vel_init: {mode: circular_orbit}` seeds near-circular orbital speeds v = spin*sqrt(G*M(&lt;r)/r)
# from the enclosed mass, plus an optional central point mass (`central_mass`). This replaces the
# former `disk_ic` operator -- placement lives in `seed_positions`, velocity in `vel_init`.
#
# TWIN of the galaxy prototype&#x27;s sweep winner bh0.5_m1_j0.06_s0.9 (N=25000, world 8, disc_R 1.5,
# central mass 0.5, disk mass 1.0, spin 0.9, jitter 0.06, softening 0.08, dt 0.004, 10000 frames).
general: {name: spiral_galaxy, seed: 2, n_frames: 10000, dt: 0.004, boundary: free, world: [8.0, 8.0]}
sets:
  star:
    n: 25000
    vel_init: {mode: circular_orbit, G: 1.0, spin: 0.90, softening: 0.08, central_mass: 0.5, jitter: 0.06}

seed:
- {op: seed_positions, at: star, mode: disc, radius: 1.5, seed: 2}
operators:
- {op: squared_law, at: star, law: gravity, k: 1.0, softening: 0.08, all_pairs: true}
schedule: [squared_law]</pre></span></span>
      <span class="sim-cap">25,000 stars, one kind of entity. One lateral activity summed over every pair. A disc condenses into a galaxy.</span>

      <span class="sim-name" tabindex="0">one kind of entity, four clumps<span class="sim-spec"><pre># nbody_cluster -- gravitational N-body collapse via the unified `squared_law` operator
# (law: gravity, all_pairs). After Philip Mocz, "Create Your Own N-body Simulation
# (With Python)" (2020), vendored at papers/nbody-python/ (MIT).
# N=10000 stars (dense), total mass ~20 (mass/star = 0.002), softened Newtonian gravity
# (k=G=1, eps=0.1), OPEN boundary. A colder start (vel_init 0.5) + smaller dt make the
# collapse into a bound, orbiting cluster read gradually rather than flashing past. Run for
# 16,000 frames (4x the first pass) because at 4,000 the cluster had only just formed: what it
# DOES once bound -- whether it stays a cluster, spins up a bar, or evaporates -- is after that.
# all-pairs O(N^2) force is fused with torch.compile (`compile: true`) so N=10000 is cheap.
general: {name: nbody_cluster, seed: 17, n_frames: 16000, dt: 0.0006, boundary: free, world: [4.0, 4.0]}
sets:
  star:
    n: 10000
    vel_init: 0.5
    types: {s: {fraction: 1.0, mass: 0.002}}         # ~20 total mass / 10000 stars
fields: {}
operators:
  - {op: squared_law, at: star, law: gravity, k: 1.0, softening: 0.1, all_pairs: true, compile: true}
schedule: [squared_law]
plotting: {background: black, point_size: 2, colors: {s: [0.7, 0.7, 1.0]}, movie_max_frames: 480}
# 480 movie frames, not the default 120: over 16,000 frames a 120-frame movie is a slideshow of
# four stills per collapse, and the two clumps merge between two of them.

# --- auto: video descriptions (gemma-4-12B) ---
descriptions:
  movie_star:
    description: A dense cluster of blue particles begins as a horizontal, elongated structure with three
      distinct peaks. Over time, the cluster undergoes a contraction and rotation, pulling inward toward
      a central point. The three peaks merge into a single, more compact and vertically oriented mass.
      By the final frame, the cluster has stabilized into a concentrated, roughly elliptical shape.
    objects: The scene contains thousands of tiny, light-blue dots representing particles. These particles
      are initially arranged in a loose, horizontal chain with three prominent concentrations. As the
      simulation progresses, the particles move closer together, changing the topology from a multi-peaked
      chain to a single unified cluster. The size of each individual particle remains constant throughout
      the entire sequence.</pre></span></span>
      <span class="sim-cap">10,000 stars in four clumps, all entities of one kind. One activity over all of them. They merge into a single cluster.</span>
    </figcaption>
  </figure>
  <figure class="sim-card">
    <video src="gallery/galaxy_collision_3d_s.mp4" autoplay loop muted playsinline preload="metadata"></video>
    <figcaption>
      <span class="sim-name" tabindex="0">two discs, one kind of entity<span class="sim-spec"><pre># galaxy_collision_3d -- TWO 3D galaxies on a grazing prograde passage. The same `squared_law`
# (law: gravity, all_pairs) that holds one disc together is what pulls the two discs into each
# other: the pair is ONE set with two types, not two sets, and that is the point -- an all-pairs
# law sums over the whole set, so mutual gravity between the galaxies is not a second operator.
#
# Initialization is the `seed_positions` operator: `mode: two_disks` places two flat discs
# `separation` apart along x, the second tilted `tilt` radians out of the first&#x27;s
# plane; `vel_init: {mode: circular_orbit}` then spins EACH disc about its own centre in its own
# plane (from that disc&#x27;s enclosed mass + its `central_mass` core) and adds the encounter velocity
# as two half-speeds -- `approach` closing along the separation axis, `swirl` tangential to it.
#
# THE ORBIT IS DESIGNED BACKWARDS FROM ITS PERICENTRE. With G = 1 and M_tot = 3.0 (two galaxies of
# core 0.75 + disc 0.75), v_rel = 2*sqrt(0.18^2 + 0.26^2) = 0.63 against the parabolic
# sqrt(2 G M_tot / 6) = 1.00, and L = 2 * 6 * 0.26 = 3.12, which is the bound orbit a = 5.0,
# e = 0.59: pericentre 2.0 = 1.7 DISC RADII, period 40.6 time units, first passage at t = 8.7 and
# the second at t = 30 -- both inside the 40 time units this run covers (10000 frames x dt 0.004).
# The angular momentum has to come from `swirl`: offsetting the discs and aiming them at each
# other leaves L = 0, and a pilot of that plunges to pericentre 0.4, shreds both discs and unbinds
# half the stars. A prograde passage at ~2 disc radii is the tail-raising case, after Toomre &amp;
# Toomre, &quot;Galactic Bridges and Tails&quot; (1972). Softened gravity is Mocz&#x27;s, vendored at
# papers/nbody-python/ (MIT).
#
# `type_layout: split_x` types the set by x, and at frame 0 the two discs are disjoint in x (each
# 2.4 wide, 6.0 apart), so the low-x disc is `red` and the high-x disc is `blue`: the colours ARE
# the two galaxies, and every later mixing of red into blue is stars changing galaxy.
general: {name: galaxy_collision_3d, seed: 2, n_frames: 10000, dt: 0.004, boundary: free, dim: 3, world: [12.0, 12.0, 12.0], record_cap: 1000}
sets:
  star:
    n: 25000
    type_layout: split_x                            # low-x disc -&gt; red, high-x disc -&gt; blue
    vel_init: {mode: circular_orbit, G: 1.0, spin: 0.90, softening: 0.15, central_mass: 0.75, jitter: 0.06, approach: 0.18, swirl: 0.26}
    types:                                          # 12500 stars per galaxy: disc mass 0.75 each
      red: {fraction: 0.5, mass: 0.00006}
      blue: {fraction: 0.5, mass: 0.00006}
fields: {}
seed:
- {op: seed_positions, at: star, mode: two_disks, radius: 1.2, thickness: 0.06, separation: 6.0, offset: 0.0, tilt: 0.6, seed: 2}
operators:
  # softening 0.15 = 1/8 of a disc radius: the pericentre is 2.0, so the two cores never come
  # near it, and halving dt to 0.002 reproduces the same trajectory to three digits.
- {op: squared_law, at: star, law: gravity, k: 1.0, softening: 0.15, all_pairs: true}
schedule: [squared_law]</pre></span></span>
      <span class="sim-cap">25,000 stars, two discs among entities of one kind. The same one activity. They raise tidal tails in one another.</span>
    </figcaption>
  </figure>
  <figure class="sim-card">
    <video src="gallery/galaxy_merger_3d_s.mp4" autoplay loop muted playsinline preload="metadata"></video>
    <figcaption>
      <span class="sim-name" tabindex="0">the same entities, head-on<span class="sim-spec"><pre># galaxy_merger_3d -- the SAME two galaxies, head-on: one knob apart from `galaxy_collision_3d`
# (`swirl: 0.26` -&gt; `0.0`), and that knob is the encounter&#x27;s angular momentum. L = 0 makes the
# orbit radial, so the pericentre is 0 instead of 2.0 disc radii: the two discs fall straight
# through each other, the cores sink and merge on the first passage, and what is left is one
# spheroidal remnant with red and blue stars mixed through it and a debris halo -- no tails, since
# there is no orbital rotation to swing the stripped stars into one. Same operator, same discs,
# same masses, same `approach`: only L differs. (`approach` 0.25 rather than 0.18 keeps |v_rel|
# 0.50 -- still half the parabolic 1.00 at separation 6, so the pair is bound.)
#
# Initialization is the `seed_positions` operator: `mode: two_disks` places two flat discs
# `separation` apart along x, the second tilted `tilt` radians out of the first&#x27;s
# plane; `vel_init: {mode: circular_orbit}` then spins EACH disc about its own centre in its own
# plane (from that disc&#x27;s enclosed mass + its `central_mass` core) and adds the encounter velocity
# as two half-speeds -- `approach` closing along the separation axis, `swirl` tangential to it.
#
# `type_layout: split_x` types the set by x, and at frame 0 the two discs are disjoint in x (each
# 2.4 wide, 6.0 apart), so the low-x disc is `red` and the high-x disc is `blue`: the colours ARE
# the two galaxies, and every later mixing of red into blue is stars changing galaxy.
general: {name: galaxy_merger_3d, seed: 2, n_frames: 10000, dt: 0.004, boundary: free, dim: 3, world: [12.0, 12.0, 12.0], record_cap: 1000}
sets:
  star:
    n: 25000
    type_layout: split_x                            # low-x disc -&gt; red, high-x disc -&gt; blue
    vel_init: {mode: circular_orbit, G: 1.0, spin: 0.90, softening: 0.15, central_mass: 0.75, jitter: 0.06, approach: 0.25, swirl: 0.0}
    types:                                          # 12500 stars per galaxy: disc mass 0.75 each
      red: {fraction: 0.5, mass: 0.00006}
      blue: {fraction: 0.5, mass: 0.00006}
fields: {}
seed:
- {op: seed_positions, at: star, mode: two_disks, radius: 1.2, thickness: 0.06, separation: 6.0, offset: 0.0, tilt: 0.6, seed: 2}
operators:
  # softening 0.15 = 1/8 of a disc radius. Here the cores DO meet, so this is what keeps the
  # core-core force finite; halving dt to 0.002 reproduces the same trajectory to three digits.
- {op: squared_law, at: star, law: gravity, k: 1.0, softening: 0.15, all_pairs: true}
schedule: [squared_law]</pre></span></span>
      <span class="sim-cap">25,000 stars, two discs among entities of one kind. The encounter head-on. They fall through each other and leave one remnant.</span>
